archetype.name: Cup Contender (play-driving)
archetype.definition: Tampa Bay controls 5-on-5 play as well as almost anyone, has elite talent at the top of the lineup and a blue line graded A, and its record rests on that rather than on bounces.

report.headline: Elite 5-on-5 process is carrying Tampa past a leaky kill and average goaltending
report.take:
Tampa Bay sits atop a crowded Atlantic at 13-5-2 and fourth on the site, and the most important thing about this team is how it is winning. The Lightning own 56.3% of the 5-on-5 expected goals and 55% of the shot attempts, both third in the league. They put 29.4 shots a game on net (5th) and allow 24.9 (7th). That is a team tilting the ice, not one living on a hot goalie or a string of one-goal escapes. Pts vs Goal Diff sits at a modest 1.3, so the standings line roughly matches a +15 differential.

The top of the forward group does the heavy lifting. Kucherov (28 points, 60.8% xGF), Guentzel (24 points, 63.6%) and Hagel (13 goals, 80 shots, 65.7%) each log over 20 minutes and drive play hard. Point and Cirelli add second-line centers who also post xGF shares above 60%. John Carlson ranks 4th of 259 on the defense tab, and Charle-Edouard D'Astous has seven power-play points. Below that it thins out. Mikheyev is under water at 48.4% xGF, Goncalves has no goals in 17 games, and J.J. Moser has one point in more than 18 minutes a night.

The numbers hide two things that run in opposite directions. Tampa's 12.6% shooting is sixth in the league and well above the 11.4% average, and the 5-on-5 PDO of 102.3 says some of the scoring will cool. Against that, two areas that have historically been strengths are underperforming badly. The penalty kill is at 71.7% (25th) after 82.6% last season. The goaltending reads as dead average: a .892 save % that exactly matches the league, Goalies GSAx of 0.5 against 12.5 a year ago, and Vasilevskiy at .889 and 26th of 71 on the goalie tab. If either of those normalizes toward Tampa's own history, it offsets any shooting regression.

The direction is good. Goals allowed per game fell from 3.31 in October to 2.29 in November. That fits a team whose shot suppression was always better than its results, and it is the strongest sign this is a contender rather than a fast starter. The pace of 115 points is probably a touch high, but the underlying profile looks like last year's 106-point team with better possession numbers.

strengths.title: Dominant 5-on-5 territorial edge
strengths.body: Tampa owns the third-best share of both expected goals and shot attempts in the league, and it out-shoots opponents comfortably in all situations. The edge is broad: every top-six forward and four of six defensemen are above 50% xGF. Process numbers like these are the most stable thing in hockey, so this should hold.

strengths.title: Star trio driving offense
strengths.body: Kucherov, Guentzel and Hagel are all top-seven players on their position tabs and each controls well over 60% of expected goals on the ice. Hagel's 80 shots show his production is volume-based rather than fluky. The concentration is a risk if one goes down, but the quality is real.

strengths.title: Defense tightening as season matures
strengths.body: Goals allowed dropped sharply from October to November, and the last five games were below the season rate. That lines up with the low shots-against numbers finally showing up on the scoreboard, so it is more signal than noise. The A-graded blue line, led by Carlson, supports it.

concerns.title: Penalty kill far off its standard
concerns.body: At 71.7% the kill ranks 25th and sits well under the league average. Tampa has run an 80%+ kill for each of the last five seasons, so this looks more like an early-season slump than a structural collapse. Still, it is the clearest way better teams can beat them this month.

concerns.title: Goaltending now neutral, not an edge
concerns.body: Tampa's goalies are saving roughly what an average goalie would, a big drop from the double-digit GSAx seasons of the past two years. Vasilevskiy's .889 trails backup Hildeby, and the group's B grade is middle-of-the-pack for a contender. If this persists, Tampa's ceiling relies entirely on out-chancing teams.

concerns.title: Hot shooting and thin depth
concerns.body: A 12.6% shooting rate and a 102.3 PDO at 5-on-5 point to some scoring cooling off. When it does, the bottom of the lineup offers little help: Goncalves has no goals and Moser has a single point despite heavy minutes.

trend.note: A good-not-great October gave way to a much stingier November, and the last 10 went 6-2-2 with a +10 differential. The play has stayed strong throughout, and results are catching up to it.

weekAhead.headline: Three home games, two soft defenses, one real test
weekAhead.body:
All three games are at home, and two come against defenses that have struggled. Washington is 28th in goals against with D-graded goaltending, and it bleeds points to wingers, where Kucherov and Hagel live. Buffalo has the league's worst all-situations PDO, a .873 save %, and the weakest defense anywhere against centers. Tampa scored eight on Buffalo just last week.

Edmonton is the headline game, and it is a fascinating contrast. The Oilers are 16-3-3 and third on the site, but they sit 24th in xGF % and 22nd in CF %. Their record rests on a league-best 15.6% shooting rate and A- goaltending. Tampa should control the play. The danger is Edmonton's 34.2% power play against Tampa's 25th-ranked kill, so staying out of the box decides that one.

keyMatchups.title: Oilers' power play vs Tampa's kill
keyMatchups.body: Edmonton converts at the third-best rate in the league while Tampa's kill is 25th. That is the single matchup most likely to flip a game Tampa otherwise should own at 5-on-5. The Oilers' underlying 5-on-5 numbers are weak, so special teams are their best path.

keyMatchups.title: Tampa wingers vs Washington
keyMatchups.body: Washington ranks 28th at holding wingers below their usual output, and its goaltending is graded D. Kucherov and Hagel, Tampa's two most productive wingers, should get chances to pad totals.

keyMatchups.title: Buffalo's goaltending and center coverage
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo's .873 save % is 28th and it is last in the league against centers. Guentzel, Point and Cirelli should find room. A short memory matters, though: Tampa was blanked 2-0 by Detroit to end last week.

weekAhead.watch: Tampa's penalty kill against Edmonton: if it holds, Tampa's 5-on-5 edge should decide the game.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is sustainable: top-three possession numbers, low shots against, and a star group producing on volume. Expect the shooting percentage to drift down toward the league norm, which would cost some goals. Expect the penalty kill and goaltending to recover toward Tampa's recent standards, which would win some of them back. Net, a team that finishes near the top of the Atlantic with a 100-plus point season looks like the base case, even if the 115-point pace overshoots.

The risk is concentration. Three forwards and Carlson carry most of the production, and the depth forwards and a couple of heavy-minute defensemen contribute little offense. An injury at the top would expose that. Otherwise this profile is better than last season's in process terms.
swingFactors: Vasilevskiy returning to above-average save rates

confidence.note: Twenty games is a modest sample, but the possession and shot numbers are stable and match recent history.
